nameStory: Sea-buckthorn gets its name from its thorny branches and its natural habitat along seacoasts, where it thrives in sandy, salt-sprayed conditions. The 'buckthorn' part refers to its spiny nature, though it's not related to true buckthorns at all. Early sailors and coastal dwellers probably noticed these hardy, spiky shrubs clinging to clifftops and dunes near the sea.
description: Sea-buckthorn is a tough, spiny deciduous shrub that looks like it means business with its thorny branches and silvery leaves. It typically grows 6-13 feet tall and wide, forming dense, somewhat scraggly colonies that can handle harsh coastal conditions. The shrub has a distinctive silvery-gray appearance from a distance, with narrow leaves that shimmer in the breeze. Female plants produce clusters of bright orange berries that persist well into winter, making them quite eye-catching against the silvery foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel smooth on top but are covered with tiny silvery scales underneath, giving them a distinctive two-toned appearance when the wind flips them over

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright orange berries clustered tightly along the branches, about the size of small peas, with a tart smell and extremely sour taste if you dare to try one

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Rough, grayish-brown bark on older stems with prominent thorns that are sharp enough to catch clothing and skin

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, thorny thickets through underground runners, often creating impenetrable colonies that lean away from prevailing ocean winds

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous yellowish flowers appear before the leaves in early spring, with male and female flowers on separate plants

habitat: In New England, sea-buckthorn is most commonly found along the immediate coastline in sandy soils, dunes, and clifftops where it can handle salt spray and harsh winds. It occasionally escapes cultivation to establish in disturbed areas inland, particularly in poor, sandy soils where few other shrubs can compete. Look for it in places where the soil drains quickly and other plants struggle to survive.

seasonality.spring: Small yellowish flowers appear in March-April before the leaves emerge, though they're easy to miss since they lack petals and are quite tiny.
seasonality.summer: Silvery-green foliage is at its most distinctive, with the two-toned leaves creating a shimmering effect in coastal breezes.
seasonality.fall: Bright orange berries ripen and become very noticeable, while leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Orange berries often persist on bare branches well into winter, making identification easier when the distinctive leaves are gone.

funFact: Sea-buckthorn berries contain more vitamin C than oranges - up to 15 times more! - which made them incredibly valuable to ancient civilizations, and legend says Genghis Khan fed the berries to his horses to keep them strong and healthy during long campaigns.
confusionNotes: The silvery, narrow leaves might remind you of Russian olive or autumn olive, but sea-buckthorn's leaves are much narrower and the bright orange berries are clustered directly on the branches rather than hanging on short stalks. The thorny, dense growth habit is also much more aggressive than these relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, sea-buckthorn isn't related to common buckthorn (the invasive species) at all - it's actually in the oleaster family. It was intentionally planted for erosion control and as an ornamental, but can spread aggressively in the right conditions, so some consider it potentially invasive in coastal New England.
compareHints: Sea-buckthorn is the only member of its genus found in New England, but it's closely related to Russian olive and autumn olive in the same family. Unlike those relatives, sea-buckthorn has much more prominent thorns, narrower leaves, and a more aggressive spreading habit through underground runners. The bright orange berries clustered tightly on branches (rather than dangling) are also distinctive among the oleaster family members.
